mcqs.question: A team sets its bundle budget to 170KB because "that's what a mid-tier Android test device needs to hit a 2.5s LCP target," rather than picking a round number. Why does this matter?
options: It doesn't matter — any consistent number works as a budget
170KB is inherently a magic number all browsers optimize for
A round number is always more strict than a measured one
A budget derived from a measured condition is defensible when someone wants to bust it, since there's a concrete reason behind the number instead of an arbitrary one
mcqs.explanation: A number backed by a real device/network measurement gives you an answer to "why not 200KB" when a feature team pushes back — an arbitrary round number has no such defense and tends to get negotiated away. There's nothing inherently special about 170 itself, and strictness isn't about roundness.

mcqs.question: A team hits its bundle-size budget every release but users still report the page feels unresponsive for a second after it visually loads. What metric is most likely being missed?
options: LCP, since the page clearly hasn't finished rendering its largest element
Request count, since bundle size has nothing to do with request count
TTI (Time to Interactive) — the page can look visually done while the main thread is still blocked and unresponsive to input
Bundle size itself, which should be re-measured with a stricter compression setting
mcqs.explanation: A small bundle can still run expensive synchronous work that blocks the main thread after paint — TTI specifically measures reliable responsiveness to input, which is exactly the gap a bundle-size-only budget misses. LCP is about visual paint, which the scenario says already looks done, and re-measuring bundle size doesn't address a responsiveness problem.

mcqs.question: Why does the CI config budget `main.*.js` and `checkout.*.js` separately instead of using one combined budget for total JS shipped?
options: Combined budgets are not supported by any CI tool
Per-chunk budgets make it clear which specific route regressed, since main (loaded on every route) needs a tighter limit than a route-specific chunk only some users load
Separate budgets are required because gzip cannot compress multiple files together
It has no real benefit — a single global number is equally informative
mcqs.explanation: A single global budget can hide which route actually grew — per-chunk tracking pinpoints the regression to main vs. a specific route, and lets main (paid by every visitor) carry a stricter limit than an occasionally-loaded chunk. Combined budgets are a real, supported pattern, gzip compresses files independently regardless, and the distinction genuinely does add diagnostic value.

mcqs.question: A team discovers one modal on their product page pulls in a 200KB charting library, opened by only 5% of visitors. What splitting approach fits this specific case best?
options: Route-based splitting, since the whole product page should be split out
No splitting — 200KB is within most route budgets so it's not worth the complexity
Rewriting the app without any charting library
Component-based splitting, isolating just the charting library so only the 5% who open the modal ever download it
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the scenario component-based splitting is for — a specific, identifiable heavy dependency used by a minority of interactions, split out surgically rather than shipped to everyone visiting the page. Route-based splitting operates at the wrong granularity here (the whole page, not the library), and dismissing the cost ignores that 95% of visitors pay for a library they never use.

mcqs.question: A team has good route-based code-splitting in place, but the bundle budget is still failing. What's a cause code-splitting alone does NOT address?
options: The initial route the user lands on being too large
Two independently-loaded routes each bundling their own separate copy of the same date library because the bundler didn't dedupe it
Users on a slow connection experiencing high latency
The main chunk being loaded on first visit
mcqs.explanation: Duplicated dependencies across chunks are a real cost that splitting doesn't fix by itself — the bundler needs help (deduplication config, or a shared-dependency policy) to avoid shipping the same library twice. The other options describe things splitting is specifically designed to help with, not gaps it leaves open.

mcqs.question: A team's CI budget check has been bumped from 170KB to 250KB three times over two years, each time as a one-off exception with no reassessment. What does this pattern indicate?
options: The budget mechanism is working correctly — bumping a number when needed is exactly its purpose
The check should be removed entirely since it clearly isn't preventing growth
The budget has effectively stopped functioning as a budget — it's being renegotiated without evidence rather than revisited on a schedule against real device/network data
250KB is now the objectively correct budget for any app
mcqs.explanation: A budget that only ever receives ad hoc bumps with no evidence-based reassessment has lost its actual function — the fix is a scheduled review against real data, not removing the check (which would remove the only signal at all) or assuming the new number is inherently correct for any product.
